title: PGE leads Pacific Northwest with first-of-its-kind wildfire research
summary: Measuring vegetation moisture is helping PGE better understand fire potential in high-risk areas and refine efforts to keep customers and communities safe.
body_markdown:
**PORTLAND, Ore.** – Portland General Electric is measuring the moisture levels in live plants to better understand how vegetation conditions influence wildfire risk. Combining hands-on field work, weather monitoring and emerging sensor technology, the research will help PGE’s wildfire operations team understand how much moisture is contained in living vegetation throughout the year.


With support from NASA's[FireSense](https://cce.nasa.gov/firesense/index.html) program and in partnership with researchers from the University of Idaho, PGE is building a more complete picture of wildfire risk across its service territory by measuring how live vegetation responds to changing weather, drought and soil conditions. This information will help PGE make better informed safety decisions to keep customers and communities safe.


### **The many factors of wildfire behavior**


Wildfire behavior depends on more than high temperatures, low humidity and strong winds. The condition of the vegetation itself plays an important role in determining how easily a fire can start, spread and intensify.


While weather conditions can be monitored continuously through remote sensors like weather stations and satellites, the moisture content of living vegetation requires more hands-on observations.


> "Wildfire not only needs the right weather conditions, but it also depends on the fuels," said Lisa Kriederman, PGE’s lead meteorologist. "We're trying to bring together all of this information, including weather station data, soil moisture, dead fuel moisture and now live fuel moisture, to get a full picture of fire risk across our service territory."


For years, wildfire professionals have relied on weather observations, drought indicators, fire danger indices and satellite products to assess wildfire conditions. While those tools remain essential, they do not always reveal how vegetation is responding to prolonged heat, drought stress or changing environmental conditions.


### **This type of research has never been done in the Pacific NW before**


One of the program's most significant contributions is the creation of a long-term dataset for Oregon and the greater Pacific Northwest.


> "We are doing this to understand climatologically what we are normally supposed to be seeing in the vegetation throughout the season," Kriederman said. "There haven’t been any historical measurements done here in the Pacific Northwest, so we saw this as an opportunity to collect this data and make it available to our partners so everyone can benefit from this missing historical record."


Over time, the data will help establish what constitutes normal seasonal drying versus unusually dry or stressed conditions.


> “When we take our samples, we follow a standardized field protocol,” said Andrew Stinchfield, PGE’s fire behavior analyst. “That’ll give us a more granular picture of what the fire danger is.”


PGE currently samples live vegetation at 11 locations where the utility already has weather stations and soil moisture monitoring equipment. Researchers are tracking the complete annual moisture cycle, from spring green-up and peak seasonal moisture through summer drying, late-season minimums and eventual recovery after seasonal precipitation returns.


### **Better informed decisions to keep communities safe**


The live fuel moisture program is part of PGE's broader wildfire risk analysis framework, which evaluates hazard exposure, infrastructure vulnerability and the potential consequences of wildfire.


Kriederman and her team monitor weather conditions year-round and draw on information from more than 100 of PGE’s weather stations across its service area. The weather station network provides highly localized information on temperature, humidity, wind, soil and dead fuel moisture and other environmental conditions. By incorporating live fuel moisture data into that existing system, PGE gains another layer of intelligence about conditions on the ground.


> “As we build out this new dataset, we’ll be able to compare vegetation moisture levels with soil moisture conditions and weather trends to identify periods when vegetation may be becoming unusually dry and more receptive to fire,” said Stinchfield.


That additional insight will help PGE, fire districts, emergency management agencies and municipalities prepare for and maintain better operational awareness during wildfire season.


### **A holistic approach to the challenge posed by wildfire**


Tackling the risk of wildfire is a team effort and it will take everyone to find a solution. As the first electric utility in the Pacific Northwest to undertake this kind of research, PGE is helping build knowledge that will benefit not only its customers, but also the broader wildfire and emergency management community across the region.


This deeper understanding of how vegetation conditions influence wildfire potential across the Pacific Northwest will help improve wildfire forecasting, strengthen operational decision-making and support efforts to reduce the likelihood and potential impacts of wildfire.
